item.title: South Korean police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c780wy7ype4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
South Korean police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work - Published A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities. The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families. Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks. The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers. On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty. In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety. A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'." One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend. At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu. Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities. Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week. In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted. The man was eventually found dead earlier this month. Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe. - Bodies found on S Korean holiday island as missing persons scandal deepens - Published6 days ago Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world. While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month. This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police. The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics. However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence. President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism. On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

item.title: Zambia's president sworn in for second term while opponent detained
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m7vp5895o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Zambia's president sworn in for second term while opponent detained - Published Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following a disputed election and the arrest of his main opponent on treason charges. Hichilema - credited with stabilising the economy - swept to victory on 13 August with 60% of the vote, according to official results. Runner-up Brian Mundubile, who received 38%, alleged that the outcome had been tampered with. He was unable to mount a legal challenge to the result as the courts were sealed off last week on the final day a case could be filed. Election observers said that while polling day was largely peaceful, some have raised questions about the vote tallying process. European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of opposition politicians. The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurrection, which they denied. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had gone into hiding. They were detained by police last week and charged at the weekend. During his inauguration speech on Tuesday, Hichilema did not comment on his opponent's detention but said that the "pursuit of political power must never come at the expense of peace, security and stability in our country". "Democracy does not require us to agree on everything. It requires us to respect one another even when we disagree," Hichilema added. He also invited the opposition to work with his government for the good of the country: "When you have a good idea, we will listen to you." He was sworn into office amid jubilant scenes, as thousands of supporters gathered to celebrate the inauguration. His running mate Mutale Nalumango was also sworn in as vice-president. Presidents from Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Tanzania were among several African leaders attending the inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital. When Hichilema, 64, came into office in 2021 after a landslide victory, the copper-rich nation had recently defaulted on its international debt and had an annual inflation rate of more than 24%. "We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka before the election. The former businessman negotiated a restructuring of the debt and rebuilt relations with foreign creditors. Inflation has also come down, but prices are still rising and many continue to struggle with the cost of living. Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations he said he laid over the past five years. "We are moving from stabilisation to growth," the president said in his inauguration in speech. "Having done the heavy lifting in our first term, the next five years is all about growth and prosperity for all our people. I will continue to be a servant president for all the people of Zambia," he added. With a recent rise in the price of copper - which the World Bank says accounts for about 15% of GDP and more than 70% of exports - investors remain confident and appear ready to overlook post-election issues, the Bloomberg news agency reports. item.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr451lpl4no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case - Published The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case. The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address. Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday. A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body. A pre-trial hearing is set for 19 October. Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to the BBC that the court had granted their request to withdraw from the case and had appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office to represent the singer. The statement said that D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel". "We continue to support David and his defence against these serious charges," they said. "We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him." Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan. Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said in a statement that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. - US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old - Published28 July Los Angeles County's top prosecutor, Nathan Hochman, said outside the courtroom on Monday that his office was "ready to proceed" with its case against Burke. He also acknowledged that the singer's change in lawyers could delay proceedings, require additional time to review the evidence, or result in the filing of a motion to dismiss the case. His team was ready for "zealous representation" by the defence, he said. Burke had already entered a not guilty plea to charges of first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse. He returned to court on Monday to have the charges against him formally read and re-entered the plea. The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence. Prosecutors allege Burke killed Hernandez because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career. Evidence read in Los Angeles court during the preliminary hearing showed threats she made against him on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl. "I swear to GOD I will kill u," one expletive-laden text from Hernandez read, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on. The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up. Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

item.title: US army secretary resigns after months of tension
item.description:

========================================
US army secretary resigns after months of tension - Published US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation after about 18 months in the role. His departure was confirmed by CBS, the BBC's US media partner, which reported it came after months of conflict between him and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The youngest-ever army secretary has often been referred to as President Donald Trump's "drone guy". Driscoll, 41, has been "highly effective" in advancing Trump's agenda "to Make America Strong Again" and provided "outstanding leadership" during military operations, the White House said in a statement given to CBS. The BBC has contacted the White House, Pentagon and Army for comment. Driscoll is the latest in a string of recent high-profile military leaders to depart, including Navy Secretary John Phelan who abruptly quit in April. Other notable departures include Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Army Gen David Hodne and Maj Gen William Green. Since entering the Pentagon, Hegseth has fired more than a dozen senior military officers, including the chief of naval operations and the Air Force's vice-chief of staff. The details of the behind-the-scenes friction between Driscoll and Hegseth are unclear but CBS notes that the army secretary is good friends with George, who was reportedly asked by Hegseth to resign. The post of army secretary is the top civilian leader of the US Army, directing active duty troops, along with the National Guard and reserve soldiers. Driscoll previously served in the Army and was an officer in 2007 before leading a cavalry platoon and deploying to Iraq for several months in 2009. As army secretary, Driscoll became known as Trump's "drone guy" due to his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies. He took on a leading role last year in talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on foreign trips and meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He's also a close ally and friend of Vice-President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School. During his tenure as head of the US Army, he was a key figure in Trump's deployment of the National Guard to US cities. He also took over the role of acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Related topics - Published25 November 2025 - Published23 April

item.title: 'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1mv5ggg1l8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus - Published Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people. Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus. She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search. "She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears. Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands. "It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled. The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island. "We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go." The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say. The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey. It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday. Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact. Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said. The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say. Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry. Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened. A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said. Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday. The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic. Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident". The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. - Published1 day ago

item.title: US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w457e7ydlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom - Published The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House can go ahead, in a victory for President Donald Trump. In a 5-4 ruling, the justices granted the Trump administration's emergency request, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted construction of an above-ground portion of the project. But Chief Justice John Roberts, a conservative, sided with the three liberal justices to dissent, writing that "construction is likely unlawful" because Congress has not approved the project. The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed the legal challenge, arguing that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction. Trump demolished the historic East Wing of the executive residence last autumn to begin building the ballroom. The White House has said the project will be "substantially" finished by November and fully completed by August 2028. On Friday, the high court had temporarily allowed construction of the 90,000 sq ft (8,400 sq m) ballroom to move forward while the justices considered the lawsuit aiming to halt it entirely. In Monday's unsigned order, the five justices who cleared the way for construction said lower courts had "likely exceeded" their authority in blocking the ballroom. While the majority did not decide on the legality of the East Wing project, they said the preservation group "lacks standing" to sue the government. They ruled that the Trump administration had established it was likely to succeed in arguing that it would "suffer irreparable harm without a stay". Chief Justice Roberts wrote in dissent: "Today's decision is no victory for the separation of powers." Reacting to the ruling, Trump posted that he was "pleased" the "baseless" lawsuit had failed to halt construction. "We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, DC," he said. Trump has long argued that the White House needs a larger events space, and more recently, that it was important for his security. The Republican president emphasised the need for the ballroom after an alleged assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April. But the National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that construction was causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark. Its position stemmed from a declaration made by preservationist Alison Hoagland, who lives in Washington DC and serves on the trust's board of trustees. Hoagland, who says she visits the neighbourhood once a month, asserted that she would "suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed". In the dissent, Roberts said the injuries claimed by Hoagland were sufficient to allow the lawsuit to go ahead. The National Trust for Historic Preservation said it was disappointed in the court's decision, but welcomed the "strong dissent" by Roberts. "Each President is a temporary steward of the People's House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress," it said in a statement. The ballroom project, along with the helipad being constructed on the South Lawn, are just part of the president's wider effort to transform Washington's cityscape. His plans include the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned "Arc de Trump" larger than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

item.title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ywd9q3ywvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London - Published Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville. The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later. Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said. "DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said. DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer. She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said. DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial. "It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said. "This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan." Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon, philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You. In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs. Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy." Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media. "A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said. ========================================
Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed woman - Published A 43-year-old Swiss man has been arrested following a shooting at a rave in Switzerland in which a woman was killed. Italian 22-year-old Maria Spinelli was killed and several others injured at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in Aarau, a town about 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich on Sunday. The shooting initiated a nearly 24-hour manhunt before Aarau cantonal police confirmed they apprehended the suspect shortly before 01:00 local time on Monday (23:00 GMT on Sunday). "The investigation into the exact sequence of events, the background and the possible motive is currently under way," police said in a statement. "At this time, it is assumed that the perpetrator acted alone." Police first received a report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at about 02:30 local time on Sunday. Spinelli died at the scene, while four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe". An eyewitness told Swiss news outlet Blick that he had "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped, initially believing they were fireworks. He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was shot. Organisers had expected 3,500 people to attend. Aarau, home to approximately 23,000 people, is less than 40km from the border with Germany, where local media reported police were supporting Swiss forces. The arrest marks a quick progression in the police investigation - on Sunday afternoon, the force in Aarau said it had no leads on the perpetrator and was unsure whether it was one person or several. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni previously said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible". Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation". Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years. The last major shooting occurred in 2001, when 14 members of the parliament and local government of Zug, near Lucerne, were killed by a gunman who then took his own life. item.title: US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z72x5z1po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks - Published Iran and the US have traded strikes after American forces attacked two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The first known US strikes on Iran since late July killed two people and injured two others, according to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which vowed "response and punishment". US Central Command (Centcom) said it took "limited, precise action" after observing Iran preparing to "launch rockets and deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz", according to its spokesperson. Iran said it had struck US military bases in Jordan in response, with Jordan's army saying it had intercepted eight missiles early on Monday morning. Iran's state TV also said the Iranian army had targeted an air base in the UAE with drones. However, the UAE's Ministry of Defence denied the reports that Al-Minhad Air Base had been targeted as "unfounded". The UAE did confirm it shot down a drone. The US strike is the first known attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July. Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through before the war began. Since the conflict began in February, the strait has effectively been closed, causing wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Iran is currently demanding that tanker traffic pass by Larak Island for checks and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (£1.5m) to cross. Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack on Larak was carried out by drones. Hours later, Iranian media carried a statement by the IRGC saying it had attacked the US bases of King Hussein and al-Azraq in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response to the Larak Island attack. Iran's foreign ministry said on Monday it "strongly condemned the American military aggression on Larak", saying the strikes on bases in Jordan were a "legitimate defence". Trump later told Fox News the US would "hit them hard" in response. Later on Monday, Centcom denied an earlier IRGC claim that a supertanker had struck sea mines and caught fire while trying to navigate the Strait of Hormuz via a route not authorised by Iran. Tasnim published a photo appearing to show a vessel on fire, but did not identify the tanker or provide further details, including when the image was taken. The BBC was unable to verify the claimed attack. "This is yet another IRGC attempt to intimidate regional commercial shipping through disinformation," Centcom said. Meanwhile Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a statement quoted by state TV: "We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors." Hours after the US strike, Trump posted apparent AI videos on Truth Social showing oil infrastructure exploding. One was captioned "Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!" in reference to a major oil terminal off the coast of Iran which Trump has threatened to take. His post did not elaborate. - Why is the Strait of Hormuz so important? - Published14 July The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. The strait is a narrow stretch of water between Iran, the UAE and Oman that is about 21 miles (33km) at its tightest point. United Nations rules allow countries to exercise control of territorial seas up to 12 nautical miles (13.8 miles) from their coastline. At the narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz and its shipping lanes lie entirely within Iran and Oman's territorial waters. Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission. Trump said last week that all mines placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship or boat deploying new mines would be destroyed. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump's claim as a "propaganda" deception. Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies. Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict. The US is also continuing a naval blockade of Iran, which has affected Iran's ability to export oil. On Saturday, Centcom said it had disabled three vessels, boarded two and redirected 82 as part of the blockade. Related topics - Published30 March - Published4 days ago - Published7 days ago

item.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qxw1qw3g7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border - Published The video lasts only seconds. A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral. For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding. What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone. Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit. "This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders." It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border. On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster. Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal. The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong. Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing. Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy. Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning. The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing. The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing. When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area. "Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC. Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together. That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck. At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood. China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes. People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear. And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices. It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day. "My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified. The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away. For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open. Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped. Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area. When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins." The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge. Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult. Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese. Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China. Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour. Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China. Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network. "Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port." Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing. The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck. "But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

item.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2zy3wdqqeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen? - Published Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine. "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday. Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response. Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy. In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war". But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy. Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead. The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored. In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country. If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly? The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses. Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades. Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries. But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association. Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs. So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats. As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war. This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine. Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table. He didn't. And he hasn't. There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations. To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied: "Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path." Polite, but vague. And non-committal. After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long. And "moving forward" at what pace? And, crucially, on which path? All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success. Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on. Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory. And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country. In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine. "After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv." While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation". - Published9 hours ago

item.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz64955d56po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen - Published India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent. If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India. Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding. Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai. It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets. MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector. Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake. Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific. More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs. "Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC. At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says. "Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited." Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth. Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago. After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology. But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle. At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country. Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal. Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India. The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India". But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC. India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says. "With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides." For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time. India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai. But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts. "Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external. "Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China." Also, India remains a tough country to do business. Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese. An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external. Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts. It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere. item.title: Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93vgv4kr49o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial - Published Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five weeks. The 36-year-old former nurse killed her three small children in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts. Charged with three counts of first-degree murder, she does not dispute killing her two sons and daughter in 2023. But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong. The prosecution, on the other hand, argues Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment. On Tuesday morning, after three days of deliberation, a jury of nine women and three men will continue to deliberate, with several options before them: - not guilty - not guilty by reason of insanity - first-degree murder - second-degree murder - manslaughter Not guilty / not guilty by reason of insanity This hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice that told her to kill the children. Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind. Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility. Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC. They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong. A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital. "The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said. First-degree murder This is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person. In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. As Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, put it to the BBC, Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if they pick this outcome. Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or cruelty or premeditation or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors. In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong. Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children. Second-degree murder This is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law. It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning. "For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said. In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole. Manslaughter The jury received yet another option when the judge allowed them to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution. A manslaughter conviction would mean Clancy unintentionally killed "by wanton and reckless conduct", which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count. The manslaughter option says that through an involuntary intoxication, in this case an overprescription of her medication, Clancy experienced a mental defect that was a mitigator in her understanding what she was doing, Hershon said. Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said. "This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said. The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

item.title: From playing Serena Williams on screen to following in her footsteps
item.description:

========================================
From playing Serena Williams on screen to following in her footsteps - Published Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open. Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'. That involved the then 12-year-old American working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus. "Being able to play the role of somebody that I looked up to for my whole life was super special," Frodin told the WTA website., external "I was honoured. She was one of the players that I looked up to most, just when I was starting to play. "She's such an inspiration to me." Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles. To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion. "I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin. "This is a huge opportunity for me to enjoy the moment, have fun and see what I can do. "The atmosphere, how loud the crowd will be, I feel like I fit well in that environment." - Venus Williams loses 15th match in row in 2am finish - Published1 day ago Frodin, who is ranked 580th in the world, worked on set with Hollywood star Smith for a few days a week over a period of six months. She has fond memories of her experience working with Oscar-winner Smith, who would always remember to bring hot water to shoots to keep Frodin warm during their cold, rainy days filming out on the courts. During that time, she became so accustomed to playing like 23-time major singles champion Serena that her coaches had to help her rediscover her natural style. "After I was done shooting, I got used to her strokes," Frodin told the US Open website. "My coaches were a bit frustrated because I naturally started to hit like her. "I picked up Serena's backhand, but I tried as much as possible to go back to my strokes." - Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit - Published1 day ago It has not taken long for Frodin to secure her maiden appearance at the sport's highest level. The 17-year-old earned a wildcard into this year's US Open women's singles competition - just as Venus Williams has done - by winning the United States Tennis Association' (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championships. It comes in a year where Frodin reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open girls' singles - her best result as a junior at a major. She also made her qualifying debut on the WTA Tour as a wildcard in Miami, and pushed former world number 35 Viktorija Golubic in a three-set loss in her first meeting with a player ranked inside the top-100. But on Tuesday, she will walk out for the biggest match of her life. "To be standing here right now and actually getting a chance to play in the main draw, it means everything," said Frodin. "[Rybakina] is number two for a reason, so I'm expecting a battle. Hopefully, I can bring out my best level against her." And, while she has never met the Williams sisters, Frodin is hoping that can change this fortnight. item.title: How the US-Canada trade war is being felt on both sides of the border
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g4r4lxx25o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts - Published The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute. Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President Donald Trump returned to the White House just over 18 months ago, and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs. Canada was one of the first countries the Trump administration hit with levies, and is one of two countries to respond with its own reciprocal measures. Currently, the US has hit Canada's key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles with tariffs, and last week imposed an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods. Canada has hit back with its own counter-tariffs on American goods, announcing on Tuesday what it calls a "dollar-for-dollar" and "strategic" retaliation designed to match the US tariffs. With no resolution in sight, how has this enduring trade war affected Canada and the US, and what could come next? Here are five charts to help break it all down. Trade war hits Ontario hardest The tariffs and counter-tariffs have hit some states and provinces harder than others. In Canada, some provinces have been more exposed to US sectoral tariffs on steel, steel derivatives, aluminium, and autos and vehicle parts that don't comply with the current North American trade deal, known as the USMCA. Ontario, the most populous province with a significant manufacturing sector, has been hardest hit by the auto and steel tariffs. Several Ontario auto parts and assembly plants have announced layoffs and production cuts, and the province is estimated to have lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs since early 2025. Metal exports from Quebec - which produces steel, copper and aluminium - fell 36% between February 2025 and 2026, and there was a 3.6% drop in employment in the sector, according to data released in July. The Royal Bank of Canada estimates that Ontario and Quebec are the most impacted by US sectoral tariffs, while Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island are the least exposed. Additional US tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods that came into effect on 22 August are expected to impact all provinces in some way, though British Columbia, Quebec and Ontario will feel the brunt. Swing states in the cross hairs The US economy is much larger and the impact of Canada's counter-tariffs won't be as stark. But some states will feel the pain of Canada's retaliation more than others, with tariffs levied on C$28bn worth of US goods from steel to furniture, cosmetics and toilet paper, as of 8 September. According to data by Statistics Canada, the swing state of Ohio will be hardest hit, with C$3.2bn - or 12% - of its exports soon to be tariffed by Canada, followed by Illinois and Pennsylvania. For Ohio, it's the tax on steel that will particularly hurt, as well as the tax on laundry machines. In Illinois, where farm equipment giant John Deere is based, it will be the new tariffs on farm and construction equipment. Derek Holt, an economist with Scotiabank, noted that Canada's counter-tariffs appear to be "very deliberately oriented" towards some swing states that could decide the US balance of power in the upcoming midterm elections. From the lowest tariff rates to one with the pack Prime Minister Carney has assured Canadians that, despite the high-profile trade fight, they face some of the lowest US tariff rates compared to other countries. But with the latest 50% tariffs imposed on a range of Canadian goods, the average effective US tariff rate on Canada is now higher than Mexico's, and is approaching the rate faced by others like the UK and Vietnam. An average effective tariffs rate reflects the average tariff paid across all imports. According to data by the Royal Bank of Canada, external, the average effective US tariff rate on Canada in June was 2.9% - the lowest among major US trade partners. It has now nearly doubled to 5.7%. By comparison, the US effective tariff on the UK is 6.2%. China still faces the highest US tariffs at an average of around 20.5%. Canada's exports are going elsewhere Canada, by the happenstance of being neighbours with the world's largest economy, is hugely reliant on US trade. Their proximity - and free trade agreements in place since the 1980s - has allowed the two countries to develop one of the world's most deeply economically integrated trading relationships. The US buys more than 70% of Canadian exports, and is a top US trading partner alongside Mexico and China. But the tariff fight has already started to shift Canadian businesses to other markets. Carney has pledged to double Canada's non-US exports over the next decade. Bank of Canada statistics suggest that Canadian firms are exporting more to countries other than the US since Trump's return to the White House in January 2025. Some businesses are adapting to find customers elsewhere. Matteo Sgaramella, who owns Toronto-based menswear clothing company Outclass, told the BBC he has started attending trunk shows in Paris instead of New York, helping him reach more customers in Europe. "The reception has been amazing," he said, adding that some European stores are particularly enthused about supporting Canadian products due to the ongoing trade war with the US. "We're kind of seen as the one country that's kind of standing up to the Americans right now," Sgaramella said. Other businesses, however, are struggling to diversify their trade, particularly in Ontario manufacturing sectors that are deeply integrated with the US. A recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out three such regions in Ontario - Oshawa, London and Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo - as being particularly vulnerable. "These cities remain heavily tied to the US market, while growth in exports outside the US has been limited or insufficient to offset broader weakness in trade activity and local economic conditions," the report said. While some businesses are lagging, foreign direct investment into Canada hit C$96.8 billion in 2025, the highest inflow of capital to the Canadian economy since 2007. Canada's economy also strongly rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.3% growth in the country's GDP, thanks to a jump in exports and domestic investment. These latest figures have warded off recession concerns, at least for now. Carney is hoping to attract even more investment. In September, his government will host the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, bringing major investors, CEOs and business leaders to Toronto for two days. Fewer jobs and less disposable income On both sides of the border, tariffs have hit jobs and disposable income. According to an analysis commissioned by Canadian American Business Council (CABC), if the US and Canada allow the USMCA to fail, there would be tens of thousands of jobs lost, primarily in the manufacturing industries directly affected by tariffs and that are highly reliant on the US market. Around 55,000 manufacturing jobs have already been lost in Canada from January 2025 to January 2026, according to Bank of Canada data. Not all figures are bad, however, as employment has steadily risen in Canadian sectors that are not vulnerable to US tariffs. But there is a risk of further Canadian job losses due to the recent 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration. Calgary-based economist Trevor Tombe estimates that a total of 90,000 jobs across Canada could be lost if these new US tariffs persist. In the US, the non-partisan Center for American Progress estimates, external that Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, placed last year on dozens of America's trade partners, have also led to tens of thousands of jobs lost manufacturing, transportation and warehousing sectors. Even for those whose jobs remain secure, the tariffs have meant higher sticker prices on everyday items. The US-based Tax Foundation estimates, external that an American household could pay $840 more on average this year due to Trump's tariffs on a number of nations, including Canada. Canada's counter-tariffs are much more targeted and are designed to limit the impact on Canadian consumers, but economists say businesses will likely now pay more to manufacture goods, as a bulk of the taxes will be applied on industrial supplies imported from the US.

item.description:

========================================
Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo A weak orangutan was found lying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island. Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands. The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species. "The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI). Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water". The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.
